title: Polaris fleet POC — queueless scale & cost tradeoffs
content:
Executive summary:
This document captures the benchmarking and analysis performed for Polaris Fleet (urban delivery routing) to validate a queueless inference topology and quantify latency tail behavior, throughput limits, and unit cost tradeoffs across model variants and GPU types. Goal: decide a default production configuration for real-time route-generation (avg 16 tokens per request) with 99th percentile latency target <= 120 ms and cost target < $1.50 per 100k tokens equivalent when running at steady 70% utilization.

What we tested (high level):
- Models: redwood-7b-v2 (fp16), redwood-13b-quant (4-bit), and a distilled redwood-3b (fp16) for fallbacks.
- Hardware: NVIDIA A100-80GB (pinned) and H100-80GB (pinned).
- Serving modes: queueless continuous batching (target batch window 6ms), fixed-batch (batch size 8, 16), and synchronous single-request (no batching) as baseline.
- Cache: prefix KV cache enabled/disabled (workload uses repeated route templates; expected cache hit 22–45%).
- Workload traces: production-sampled trace from Polaris (24h sample), synthetic microbursts (Poisson base + spikes), and ramp concurrency sweep (1 -> 256 concurrent request tokens).

Test matrix and key knobs:
- Concurrency sweep: 1, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256 concurrent producers.
- Sequence lengths: 6, 16, 48 tokens per request (focus 16 tokens for main results).
- Batching windows: 0ms (sync), 6ms, 12ms.
- KV cache hit simulated: 0%, 25%, 40%.
- Replicas: single-replica experiments (multi-replica scaling left to follow-on tests).

Methodology notes:
- Each cell = average of 3 runs at steady-state for 5 minutes after warmup.
- Latency measurements: p50, p95, p99 measured at request granularity including network serialization overhead (~0.6ms measured on test harness).
- Throughput: measured in requests/sec and tokens/sec achievable while keeping p95 under 120ms.
- Cost model: GPU hourly amortized cost used A100=$3.60/hr, H100=$7.50/hr (list-rate equivalent), plus estimated infra overhead of 12%. Converted to $ per 100k tokens using measured tokens/sec under 70% utilization.

Results (selected highlights for 16-token median workload):
1) A100, redwood-7b-v2, queueless (6ms window), KV cache 25%:
- Concurrency 32: p50=18ms, p95=82ms, p99=142ms, throughput=360 req/s (5760 tok/s)
- Concurrency 64: p50=20ms, p95=110ms, p99=210ms, throughput=680 req/s (10880 tok/s)
- Cost @70% util: $1.12 per 100k tokens
- Notes: p99 crosses target at ~32–64 concurrency depending on burstiness; KV cache reduced p95 by ~14% vs no-cache.

2) H100, redwood-13b-quant, queueless (6ms), KV cache 25%:
- Concurrency 32: p50=22ms, p95=96ms, p99=188ms, throughput=410 req/s (6560 tok/s)
- Concurrency 64: p50=26ms, p95=132ms, p99=278ms, throughput=780 req/s (12480 tok/s)
- Cost @70% util: $1.38 per 100k tokens
- Notes: H100 gave higher peak throughput for the bigger model, but p99 penalties were larger under microbursts without adaptive batching throttles.

3) A100, redwood-3b (fallback), sync single-request:
- p50=9ms, p95=28ms, p99=48ms, throughput (sync per-worker) limited; used as fast fallback to keep user-visible latency when larger model p99 spikes. Cost $0.42 per 100k tokens if used as primary.

4) Fixed-batch (size 16) vs queueless (6ms):
- Fixed batch reduced p99 at low concurrency but increased median latency by ~12–18ms due to batching delay; queueless hits better median with comparable p95 when batch window tuned to 6ms.

5) Cache impact: 40% hit rate case improved p95 by ~20% and throughput by ~18% across configs (big win for templated route responses).

Key observations and root causes:
- Tail latency is dominated by two factors: intra-batch stragglers (long attention/block kernel runs on some sequences) and GPU memory pressure leading to occasional paging overhead when KV cache is disabled and model weight activations spike (noted primarily on H100 with redwood-13b-quant).
- Queueless low-latency continuous batching (6ms window) strikes a good tradeoff for this workload: keeps median low while letting opportunistic batching amortize kernel startup.
- Larger models provide higher throughput at scale but are more sensitive to burstiness and produce larger p99 tails; a dynamic fallback strategy to redwood-3b for top-of-funnel requests keeps user-visible latency low while maintaining quality for post-acceptance expansions.

Recommendations for Polaris production POC (prioritized):
1) Default runtime: A100 with redwood-7b-v2 in queueless continuous-batching mode with 6ms target window; enable prefix KV cache with target hit >=25%. Rationale: meets p95 target at expected concurrency and cost target at 70% utilization.
2) Implement a two-tier model policy: prefer 7b; on p95 degradation (observed by SLO metrics) route to distilled 3b for immediate responses and then re-hydrate a 13b-quant async scoring path for quality check/long running outputs.
3) Add batch-throttling guardrails: when queue length spikes, cap batch window growth and trigger lighter-weight model fallback instead of allowing queue to grow unbounded.
4) Instrumentation: add per-token kernel timing histograms and per-request KV cache hit tags to telemetry; expose p99 contributors in console route dashboard.
5) Cost controls: adopt model-variant routing by customer-tier to limit H100 usage to premium customers / offline heavy workloads.

Risk and mitigations:
- Risk: Real production burst shapes may include correlated long-context requests (48+ tokens) that degrade p99. Mitigation: reserve a small pool of dedicated workers pinned to 3b for cold fallback and apply request-level length-based routing.
- Risk: Quantized model instability at extreme batch sizes. Mitigation: cap batch size for 13b-quant and use gradual increase ramp tests in staging.

Next steps / action items:
- Marcus Reed: prototype routing policy + canary for redwood-3b fallback (due 2027-08-09).
- Elena Varga: add KV cache hit tags and kernel timing histograms to telemetry (due 2027-08-12).
- Priya Desai: update Polaris POC proposal with recommended default topology and cost estimate for procurement (due 2027-08-05).
- SE team: run multi-replica scaling sweep (2->16 replicas) to validate autoscaling behavior under the same workload (owner: Omar Haddad, due 2027-08-20).

Appendix: raw numbers (selected) for 16-token workload, queueless 6ms, KV25%:
- A100 / redwood-7b-v2: concurrency 32 -> p50 18ms / p95 82ms / p99 142ms / 360 req/s
- A100 / redwood-7b-v2: concurrency 64 -> p50 20ms / p95 110ms / p99 210ms / 680 req/s
- H100 / redwood-13b-quant: concurrency 32 -> p50 22ms / p95 96ms / p99 188ms / 410 req/s
- H100 / redwood-13b-quant: concurrency 64 -> p50 26ms / p95 132ms / p99 278ms / 780 req/s

Notes on reproducibility:
- Test harness and scripts committed to PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/perf-harness/pull/114
- Environment: Ubuntu 22.04, driver 535.xx, CUDA 12.2, Triton runtime 2.1. Benchmarks include a synthetic network delay injection of 0.6ms to mimic on-prem network.

Closing remark:
Polaris workload (short templated route outputs) is a strong candidate for queueless continuous-batching on A100 with a small fallback path. The combination of KV caching and a two-tier model policy unlocks predictable p95 behavior while keeping unit cost within Polaris procurement goals.
